title: Birthmarks & vascular lesions

what: ‘Birthmark’ covers several unrelated lesions. Sorting them into **vascular** and **pigmented** groups, and the vascular ones into **tumours** and **malformations**, tells you the natural history and what to do.

head: Group
Lesion
Natural history
rows: Vascular tumour
**Infantile haemangioma** (‘strawberry mark’)
Absent or faint at birth. Rapid growth in months 1–3, mostly complete by ~5 months. Slow involution over years, sometimes leaving fibrofatty tissue or telangiectasia
Vascular malformation
**Port-wine stain** (capillary malformation)
Present at birth. **Permanent**; grows with the child and may darken and thicken in adulthood
Vascular (fading)
**Salmon patch** (naevus simplex, ‘stork mark’)
Pink patch on the nape, glabella or eyelids. Facial ones usually fade in the first 1–2 years; nape ones often persist
Vascular (functional)
**Naevus anaemicus**
Pale patch caused by local vasoconstriction, not pigment loss. Permanent
Dermal melanocytosis
**Mongolian spot** (lumbosacral), **naevus of Ota** (face), naevus of Ito (shoulder)
Mongolian spots usually fade by ~4 years. Ota and Ito persist
Pigment / hamartoma
**Becker naevus**, **achromic naevus**, **linear epidermal naevus**, congenital melanocytic naevus
Stable or grow in proportion with the child. Becker naevus darkens and becomes hairy around puberty

list: **Infantile haemangioma:** a benign **clonal proliferation of endothelial cells** that stain **GLUT-1 positive** (this separates it from malformations on histology). It is the most common tumour of infancy (about 4–10%). Risk factors: **prematurity, low birth weight, female sex, multiple pregnancy** and placental anomalies.
**Port-wine stain:** a congenital malformation of dilated dermal capillaries, often from a somatic **GNAQ** mutation. It does not proliferate.

**Dermal melanocytosis** (Mongolian spot, naevus of Ota): melanocytes that **stopped in the dermis** during embryonic migration. Deep pigment looks blue-grey (Tyndall effect). GNAQ/GNA11 mutations are described in Ota.
**Achromic naevus:** a stable mosaic defect in melanin production or transfer. Melanocytes are present, unlike in vitiligo.
**Naevus anaemicus:** dermal vessels in the patch are hypersensitive to catecholamines and stay constricted. Melanin is normal.
**Becker naevus:** mosaic overgrowth of epidermis, melanocytes and hair follicles, switched on by androgens at puberty.
**Epidermal naevus:** postzygotic mosaic mutations (e.g. FGFR3, PIK3CA, HRAS) causing keratinocyte overgrowth along **Blaschko’s lines**.

head: Type
Appearance
rows: Superficial
Bright red, raised, well-defined, lobulated (‘strawberry’)
Deep
Bluish, rubbery, warm swelling under normal or bluish skin; may appear later and grow for longer
Mixed
Both components
Involuting
Greying and whitening from the centre, softening and flattening

list: Often starts as a pale, telangiectatic or bruise-like **precursor patch** in the first weeks.
Head and neck are common. Location and size matter more than appearance.
**Segmental** facial lesions (plaque-like, covering a facial segment) carry a risk of **PHACE** (posterior fossa, haemangioma, arterial, cardiac and eye anomalies).
A **white or grey surface** on a growing lesion can herald **ulceration**, especially in the nappy area, lips and neck folds.
**Five or more** skin haemangiomas suggest possible liver haemangiomas.

head: Lesion
Key features
rows: Port-wine stain

Flat, sharply demarcated pink to purple patch present at birth, often unilateral or segmental. Facial **V1 (forehead / upper eyelid)** involvement raises the possibility of **Sturge–Weber** syndrome. Limb stain with overgrowth suggests Klippel–Trénaunay-type syndromes
Salmon patch
Faint pink, often midline (nape, glabella, eyelids), darkens with crying
Mongolian spot
Flat **blue-grey** patch over the sacrum and buttocks, normal skin texture, present at birth. Common in East Asian, African, South Asian and other darker skin types
Naevus of Ota
Unilateral, mottled blue-grey or brown patches over the forehead, temple and around the eye (V1/V2). May involve the **sclera**. Present at birth or appears around puberty
Achromic naevus
Off-white patch with irregular, serrated border, present from early life. Stable, grows in proportion. Wood’s lamp: off-white, not chalk-white
Naevus anaemicus
Pale patch that **does not redden when rubbed** while the surrounding skin flushes. Under a glass slide (diascopy) it becomes indistinguishable from surrounding skin
Becker naevus
Large unilateral tan-brown patch on the shoulder or upper trunk, mostly in males. Becomes **hairy** after puberty; acne may occur within it
Linear epidermal naevus
Brown, warty, linear plaque along Blaschko’s lines, usually unilateral. **ILVEN** variant is red and itchy, often on a leg

list: **Clinical** in almost all cases. Take a history of timing: present at birth (malformation, dermal melanocytosis) or appeared and grew in the first weeks (haemangioma).
**Photograph with a ruler** at every visit. Serial photos are the best tool for growth decisions.
Ultrasound (specialist) for deep lesions or uncertainty between haemangioma, malformation and other masses. MRI for large segmental facial lesions (PHACE work-up).
**≥5 haemangiomas:** specialist will arrange abdominal ultrasound for liver lesions.
**Rub test and diascopy** separate naevus anaemicus (vascular) from hypopigmentation. **Wood’s lamp** helps separate achromic naevus from vitiligo.
Several ash-leaf-shaped pale macules: consider **tuberous sclerosis** and look for other signs.
Mongolian spot and other dermal melanocytosis: record **site, size and colour** in the notes and the red book. This protects the family from later misinterpretation as bruising.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: Infantile haemangioma vs **port-wine stain**
Haemangioma appears after birth, is raised and grows fast, then involutes. Port-wine stain is flat, present at birth and permanent
Congenital haemangioma (RICH / NICH)
Fully formed **at birth**, then either rapidly involutes or stays unchanged. GLUT-1 negative. Specialist
Venous or lymphatic malformation
Soft, compressible, persistent; no growth phase. Imaging differs
Pyogenic granuloma
Later onset (months to years); small, pedunculated, bleeds easily
Mongolian spot vs **bruising**
Bruises are tender, have a history, and change colour over days. Mongolian spots are present at birth, flat and unchanged on review
Naevus of Ota vs melasma / blue naevus
Melasma is bilateral, brown, acquired and hormone-driven. Blue naevus is a small discrete papule
Achromic naevus vs **vitiligo**
Achromic naevus is present early, stable and off-white. Vitiligo is acquired, progressive and chalk-white on Wood’s lamp
Naevus anaemicus vs hypopigmentation / pityriasis versicolor
Rub test: naevus anaemicus does not flush. [Pityriasis versicolor](condition:pityriasis-versicolor) has fine scale
Becker naevus vs café-au-lait macule / congenital naevus
Café-au-lait is smaller, smooth, no hair; ≥6 suggests NF1. Congenital melanocytic naevus is present at birth and often raised
Epidermal naevus vs viral warts / lichen striatus
Epidermal naevus is linear, present early and persistent. Lichen striatus is acquired and fades over months. Do **not** treat as warts with destructive OTC products

management: The primary-care role is **recognise, document, reassure and refer at the right time**. Treatment of complicated haemangiomas and laser for birthmarks are specialist services.

management.h: Infantile haemangioma: who to refer, and when

management.title: Refer early (ideally by about 4 weeks of age) to paediatric dermatology / vascular anomalies if any of:
list: **Periocular** (risk of amblyopia and visual loss)
**‘Beard’ distribution** (chin, jaw, neck), noisy breathing or stridor: risk of **airway** haemangioma. Urgent
**Lip or perioral** (feeding problems, ulceration, disfigurement)
**Nasal tip, ear** or large facial lesion (permanent deformity)
**Large segmental facial** lesion (PHACE work-up) or lumbosacral segmental lesion (spinal anomalies)
**Nappy area or skin folds** (ulceration)
Ulcerated, bleeding, or growing rapidly
**Five or more** skin lesions (liver screening)
Breast area in girls, or a large lesion with significant parental concern
**Low-risk small lesions:** active observation with dated photos. Explain the natural history: growth mostly in the first 3–5 months, then slow involution over years. Most need no treatment.
Do not delay referral hoping it will go away. The **early growth window** is when treatment works best.

**Oral propranolol** is first line for problematic haemangiomas. It is **specialist-initiated** with baseline assessment and dose titration. Counsel parents to give it **with or just after feeds**, and to **withhold it if the baby is unwell, vomiting or not feeding** (risk of hypoglycaemia). Report wheeze, cold peripheries, sleep disturbance or lethargy.
**Topical timolol** (off-label) is used for selected small, thin, superficial lesions on specialist advice.
**Ulcerated haemangioma:** non-adherent dressings, barrier ointment in the nappy area, analgesia, and antibiotics if infected, under the specialist plan.
Laser or surgery for residual skin changes later in childhood.
Reassure for small, uncomplicated stains. Pulsed-dye laser is a specialist option and often works better when started early in childhood.
**Facial V1 stain:** refer for ophthalmology (glaucoma) and neurology assessment (Sturge–Weber). **Limb stain with overgrowth or leg-length difference:** refer.
Cosmetic camouflage (e.g. via Changing Faces skin camouflage services) for older children and adults.
**Mongolian spot:** no treatment. Reassure that most fade by early childhood. **Document clearly.**

**Naevus of Ota:** benign. **Ophthalmology** review if the eye is involved (glaucoma). Q-switched or picosecond laser and camouflage are specialist or cosmetic options. Refer any new nodule within it.
**Achromic naevus and naevus anaemicus:** no treatment needed. Camouflage if wanted. Refer if several ash-leaf-type macules or other features of tuberous sclerosis or NF1.
**Becker naevus:** reassure. Sun protection reduces contrast. Hair removal options; laser is unpredictable for the pigment. Check for breast or pectoral under-development if extensive.

**Epidermal naevus:** emollients for small stable lesions. Refer if extensive, inflamed (ILVEN), on the scalp (sebaceous naevus), or with eye, neurological or skeletal features (epidermal naevus syndrome).
**Congenital melanocytic naevus:** large or giant lesions, multiple satellites or overlying the spine need specialist review.

management.title: Support for families
management.text: The **BAD patient information leaflet** on haemangioma of infancy and the **Birthmark Support Group** are useful signposts. Visible birthmarks can carry a real psychosocial burden as children reach school age.

red_flags: Haemangioma near the **eye**, in a **beard** distribution or with **noisy breathing**, on the **lip, nose or ear**, large **segmental**, in the **nappy area**, ulcerated or bleeding: refer early or urgently.
**Five or more** cutaneous haemangiomas (possible liver involvement).
Lumbosacral midline haemangioma or other midline lumbosacral marks (possible spinal dysraphism).
Naevus of Ota with **scleral or eye** involvement, or a **new nodule** in any pigmented birthmark.
A baby on propranolol who is not feeding, vomiting, drowsy or wheezy.
Blue-grey marks that **change** between visits, are tender, or do not fit the history: think bruising and follow safeguarding procedures.
pearls: **Tumour vs malformation:** haemangiomas come and go; port-wine stains stay. Get this right and the counselling follows.
Early referral matters. Most haemangioma growth happens by **3–5 months**, so a 6-month referral can miss the window.
A white surface on a growing haemangioma is an early warning of ulceration.
Propranolol counselling: give with feeds, and **skip the dose if the baby is not feeding**.
**Write it down:** site, size and colour of Mongolian spots and other dermal melanocytosis, in the notes and the red book.
Rub test: naevus anaemicus stays pale while the surrounding skin flushes.
**Skin of colour:** dermal melanocytosis is common, and haemangiomas can look darker or more purple. Rely on the growth history.

summary: Separate the **tumour** (infantile haemangioma: grows, then involutes) from the **malformations** (port-wine stain: permanent). Refer high-risk haemangiomas early for propranolol, and document blue-grey dermal melanocytosis clearly. Most pigmented and pale birthmarks only need reassurance.

hero.alt: AI timeline of infantile haemangioma: appearance, rapid growth, plateau and involution

glance.think: A red mark that appears in the first weeks and **grows fast** (haemangioma). A flat red-purple stain **present at birth** that grows only with the child (port-wine stain). Blue-grey, brown or pale patches that stay stable.
glance.engine: Haemangioma = clonal endothelial tumour (GLUT-1 positive). Port-wine stain = malformed dermal capillaries. Pigmented birthmarks = misplaced dermal melanocytes or mosaic overgrowth.
glance.backbone: Photograph, measure and document. Reassure for low-risk lesions. **Refer high-risk haemangiomas early** (ideally by about 4 weeks of age) so propranolol can start in the growth window.
glance.never_miss: Periocular, airway (‘beard’), lip, large facial segmental, ulcerated or multiple (≥5) haemangiomas. Facial V1 port-wine stain (Sturge–Weber). Eye involvement in naevus of Ota.
